label: Q3 2026 (Jul–Sep)
asOf: close of $124.80 on 6 Nov 2026; $112.89 before the report (5 Nov)
headline: EBITDA up 50% in a year and 2027 guidance another 10% higher, yet the stock is a quarter below July: after the election, the market fears limits on data-center power

points.t: ERCOT and PJM both set peak-demand records in July, lifting realized energy and capacity prices; the acquired Lotus plants contributed a full quarter and Martin Lake Unit 1 returned to service. Texas EBITDA rose 57% and East 36%.

About 98% of 2027 generation is hedged, so the $7.7–8.5B guide is little affected by power-price swings. Cogentrix joined in October; earlier reports said the Meta power agreement could add about $0.7B once closed, which isn't in guidance yet.
A new $1.5B authorization leaves about $2.5B through end-2028. Since 2021 it has bought back about $6.7B, cutting the share count by about 30%.

reaction: Stock: closed at $124.80 on report day (6 Nov), up 10.6%, while peers (average of Constellation and Talen) rose about 5.7%, a lead of about 5 points. Earlier, on 4 Nov (after the midterm results) it fell 13.8% in a day on fears that a Democratic Congress would limit data-center power use and prices. We found no reliable quarterly EBITDA consensus, so this page compares against company guidance.

segments.title: Segments
segments.take: Growth came mainly from the Texas and East plants: higher energy and capacity prices and acquired plants. Retail is seasonally weak in summer.

rows.why: ERCOT demand hit a record in July, raising realized prices; Martin Lake Unit 1 (coal) returned to service. The Comanche Peak nuclear plant is in Texas.
PJM capacity prices rose sharply and the acquired Lotus gas plants contributed a full quarter. PJM is the US grid with the most data centers (Northern Virginia).
Retail earns least in summer (when wholesale power costs most); its profit comes mainly in winter and spring.

segments.note: Shares are of the five-segment total before corporate and asset-closure items (about $2.38B), approximate.

extras.title: Where it sits in the AI loop
extras.take: Vistra is one of the largest US independent power producers, with nuclear, gas and coal. AI data centers need round-the-clock power, which is what Vistra sells.

items.w: It already has long-term nuclear power deals with AWS and Meta; this quarter the 405 MW Pulaski solar plant started up under a Microsoft agreement, and the Odessa gas plant signed a 20-year, 207 MW deal with New Era.
Data centers have pushed PJM capacity auction prices sharply higher, directly lifting East plant revenue.

With Democrats controlling Congress, the market fears federal or state limits on data-center hookups or caps on energy and capacity prices. PJM has already put a cap and floor on its capacity auctions.
With KKR, NVIDIA and others it formed Helix Digital Infrastructure, committing up to $1B to turn land and power next to its plants into data-center campuses.

extras.title: Where growth comes from
extras.take: Vistra grows on higher energy and capacity prices, acquired plants and long-term data-center deals, while spending heavily on buybacks. The real variable is whether policy pushes prices down.

items.w: Cogentrix's gas plants joined in October, mostly outside Texas; with the Lotus plants, its gas fleet is much larger.
About 100% of 2026, 98% of 2027 and 78% of 2028 is hedged. Near-term price swings matter little; market prices matter more from 2028.
The 2027 FCFbG midpoint of $4.7B is about 11% of today's market value; buybacks and dividends are the main uses.
The 2027 midpoint is about 11% above 2026 and excludes the Meta agreement's contribution once closed.
PJM capacity caps or federal price limits; a pause in data-center construction; lower Texas power prices (forwards have been soft); a gas-price spike squeezing margins.

trends.why: A record in the summer peak quarter, +50% in a year
Lifted by capacity prices and acquisitions

valuation.take: On the 2027 FCFbG midpoint, the market value is only about 9 times free cash flow (an 11% yield), and EV/EBITDA about 7.3x (2027). The low price reflects policy risk, not results: hedged profits are being discounted.

steps: About 330M shares after buybacks → about $14.2 a share
forward.note: FCFbG is free cash flow “before growth”: it deducts maintenance capex and interest but not new plants or acquisitions.

scenarios.note: Bear: policy pushes capacity prices down and Texas power prices fall, below the guidance range; base: guidance midpoint; bull: new agreements such as Meta close, above the top of the range. These assumptions are ours and are not forecasts.

pricezone.sub: 2027 FCFbG per share × our multiple; price at the 6 Nov close
pricezone.why: The price is inside the zone: buying at $125, the base case gains about 26% and the bear case loses about 18%, a reward/risk of about 1.4. At the $130 top of the zone it is about 1.0, at the $118 midpoint about 2.5, and the $105 low end is close to the bear price. Eleven times free cash flow is still below what the market paid in 2025; the risk is policy, not the hedged profits.

history.title: Against its own past
history.sub: P/S (TTM revenue, diluted shares), last 20 quarter ends
history.note: A power producer's revenue swings with prices, so P/S is only a rough guide: below 1x before 2023, 2–4x after the AI-power theme took off in 2024, and about 2.1x now, near the five-year median. Calculated from SEC XBRL quarterly revenue, diluted shares and Nasdaq quarter-end closes (Q3 revenue from the release).

cash.title: Adjusted EBITDA
cash.note: After the Cogentrix acquisition, liquidity fell to about $5.4B pro forma. In the first three quarters it spent $917M on buybacks, $231M on common dividends and $117M on preferred dividends.

ret.note: After the new $1.5B authorization, about $2.5B remains, to be used by end-2028, about 6% of market value at today's price. Buybacks have always been Vistra's main cash return, with dividends a small share; the share count is down about 30% since 2021.

insider.title: Effective trades 30 days around the report
insider.text: There were two executive sales in the 30 days before the report (10/7–11/6): retail president Scott Hudson sold about $3.56M on 7 Oct and CFO Kristopher Moldovan about $3.30M on 8 Oct, both under preset 10b5-1 plans, so neither counts as effective.
